chapter: Woody Herman, Condon's and Buddy Rich
title: Lean years after Condon's closed in 1985
summary: His sons go to college, work thins, and he plays with Anita O'Day, runs a Marco Island band and gets the Buddy Rich call.

story.theme_name: Making a living: hard times, day jobs and scarce work
story.community_name: Day jobs: musicians working outside music

blocks.x: What were the toughest economic years for you, as far as gigs?

I don’t remember. Well Eddie Condon’s closed in 1985. Both of my sons graduated from high school in 1985 and went to college in 1985. And there was a little lull in there that was a little nerve wracking. But my one son, the bassist, got a full paid scholarship to the Boston Conservatory, so that helped. The other one went to Manhattan School of Music and then decided he wanted to become a physicist so that took care of that. And I was working various jobs in New York and then Anita O’Day came into the game. And then I was with her. That was a funny one. Well then — oh I went to Florida for a few years, I ran the band down there at Marco Island, Florida. And that was fun for a while. I brought Steve Marcus down. But then the Buddy Rich band came and I got the call. I played Carnegie Hall with that band. But I mean that was kind of ridiculous. I mean I did the Blue Note with them and some jobs with that band. But I never, to be honest with you, I mean the guy, Buddy Rich was a freak of nature. There’s no question about that. But I never even listened to that band’s music particularly because I said I’m never going to have to play with that band.
